title: Samsung Electronics shares slid despite record profit in the third-quarter
description: The Samsung logo, representing the South Korean multinational manufacturing conglomerate, the largest chaebol of South Korea, and the world's largest
body: The Samsung logo, representing the South Korean multinational manufacturing conglomerate, the largest chaebol of South Korea, and the world's largest information technology company, consumer electronics maker, chipmaker, and smartphone manufacturer, appears on their pavilion during the Mobile World Congress 2025 in Barcelona, Spain, on March 5, 2025. (Photo by Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesSouth Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported third-quarter operating profit that is broadly in line with analysts' expectations, as demand for advanced memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications continued to grow.Following the announcement, Samsung shares were trading 5% lower. The company plans to increase sales of advanced memory chips used in AI applications and secure long-term contracts to meet growing demand.Here are Samsung's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:Revenue: 195.25 trillion won ($124 billion) vs. 195.79 trillion won expected Operating profit: 107.44 trillion won vs. 107.66 trillion won expected  Samsung's revenue rose 126.88% year-on-year and 13.85% from the previous quarter, while operating profit rose 783.11% from a year earlier.The company also announced 30 trillion won in cash dividends for the third quarter, equivalent to 4,601 won per common and preferred share.The company plans to return another 55 trillion to 75 trillion won to shareholders this year through dividends and share buybacks, as the board will finalize the total shareholder returns and specific execution plans at a meeting scheduled for late January 2027.Samsung said it became the first global technology company to top 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit, while posting record revenue and profit for a fourth straight quarter.Its semiconductor business reported 147.1 trillion won in revenue and 106.5 trillion won in operating profit, driven by strong demand for AI-related memory chips.Furthermore, its memory business also achieved record quarterly revenue and operating profit, supported by a significant ramp-up in HBM4 sales and growing demand for server solid-state drives.However, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, appeared unaroused by the numbers, as the results failing to generate much enthusiasm in the market.The market still was not impressed.Josh GilbertAPAC Lead Analyst, eToro"Investors have been so spoilt by the AI trade that a record result is now treated as the bare minimum rather than a reason to celebrate," Gilbert said, adding that Samsung's chip business accounted for nearly all of its operating profit in the third quarter, highlighting its growing reliance on memory chips."For all the talk of Samsung being a diversified giant, anyone holding the stock today is really holding a memory maker with a phone business attached," he said, stating that the company's fortunes now depend heavily on memory prices.Looking ahead, the company expects AI infrastructure investment to accelerate in 2027, with rising demand likely to further tighten memory supply. Samsung also plans to increase sales of HBM, a type of high-performance memory used in AI chips, along with other memory products used in servers and data storage. In the third quarter, Samsung Electronics and five of its affiliates had announced a combined $1 billion investment in KKR-backed Helix Digital Infrastructure. Samsung Electronics will invest $500 million, with the remaining amount coming from its affiliates.The tech giant had also announced a partnership with French AI startup Mistral AI to use AI technologies in its semiconductor operations, including chip design and manufacturing. The company also led Mistral's Series D funding round.

schema.headline: Samsung Electronics shares slid despite record profit in the third-quarter

title: Here is what changed in the new Fed statement
description: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks to reporters during his first news conference since taking the helm at the central bank on June 17, 2026 in W
body: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks to reporters during his first news conference since taking the helm at the central bank on June 17, 2026 in Washington, DC. Chip Somodevilla | Getty ImagesThis is a comparison of Wednesday's Federal Open Market Committee statement with the one issued after the Fed's previous policymaking meeting in September.Text removed from the September statement is in red with a horizontal line through the middle.New text that's been added since the last statement is in red and underlined.Black text appears in both statements.

schema.headline: Here is what changed in the new Fed statement

title: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation
description: watch nowThe Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflatio
body: watch nowThe Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflation despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee kept the overnight funds rate in a range between 3.75%-4%, where it has been since the central bank approved a quarter percentage point increase in September."Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."Two voters dissentedTwo of the 12 FOMC voters dissented from the decision – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both of whom wanted the committee to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.Cook has been at the center of a continuing controversy in which President Donald Trump has tried to remove her from office over allegations concerning information she provided on home loan applications. While the Supreme Court stopped the president's attempts, the administration has restarted the move, with a hearing scheduled for early November.This was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed in 2022 as an appointee of President Joe Biden.Dallas President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis President Neel Kashkari both joined Hammack in voting no the last time the committee held, in July, and both have expressed the need for higher rates. However, they fell in with the majority Wednesday.The midterm elections have lingered over the decision. Pivotal votes take place nationwide on Nov. 3, with control of Congress at stake. Fed officials consider political independence to be a cornerstone of the central bank, but some observers have speculated that officials won't want to raise rates this close to an election.Trump, who nominated Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to the position, has been at odds with the Fed for years. Trump has charged that the funds rate should be much lower.The dissents reflected underlying conflict on the committee over how aggressively it needs to raise rates to combat rising prices. Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and the pace of price increases has only picked up since the September meeting.Statements over the past several weeks, though, have reflected a desire to wait for additional data to come in before tightening policy further. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams both said current economic conditions allow policymakers time to evaluate their next move.The statement characterized economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace," a seeming upgrade from "solid" in September. There were no other substantial changes to the statement other than the removal of a sentence that explained the September increase.The decision came as little surprise as markets had been pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Following the decision, the S&P 500 held on to its gains. However, it raises fresh questions about how long policymakers are willing to wait before tightening again. Futures market pricing indicates a strong possibility of another hike at the next FOMC meeting in December, and perhaps another increase or two in 2027.Separately, Warsh unveiled at a news conference changes to the FOMC meetings next year that could reduce the number of rate-setting meetings each year. "We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said. "The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in 2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for setting policy."Complicated economic pictureThe Fed is up against a complicated economic and political picture. Inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred gauge is expected to be above 3% for September, even when excluding volatile food and energy prices. Economists are concerned that inflation has broadened beyond the energy sector and the impact from the Iran war.At the same time, the unemployment rate has remained low and economic growth has been strong. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker is pointing to 3.4% annualized growth in the third quarter, which would be the strongest in a year. Consumer spending also has been solid, and investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom has helped keep the U.S. economic engine running.The combination, though, has added to debate about how much restriction the Fed's current interest rate is actually exerting on the economy, and whether policymakers will need to move more aggressively if the price data doesn't improve.While markets expect additional hikes, Warsh has avoided providing so-called forward guidance about the FOMC's intentions. In June, his fellow committee members, through the "dot plot" grid, indicated the likelihood of another increase this year."The Fed is taking a wait-and-see approach, and I think that makes sense given where we are in the cycle," said Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst. "The economy is slowing, but slowing and breaking are two different things. Holding rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess how the economy is responding to September's hike and the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs."

schema.headline: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation

title: Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year
description: DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday
body: DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter.The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year. "This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday.Ford reported third-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $4.7 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than what analysts were anticipating, according to StreetAccount.Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:Earnings per share: 49 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expectedAutomotive revenue: $46.08 billion vs. $46.24 billion expectedThe Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion.House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs.House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison.She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models."Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said.Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter.Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027.The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year.The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount.As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance. It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026.Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion. Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion.Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.

schema.headline: Ford reports mixed third-quarter results, says 2027 earnings will be in line with this year

title: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
description: Signage for a Wendy's restaurant in Brampton, Ontario, on April 21, 2026. Mike Campbell | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA group of investors led by Nelson Pe
body: Signage for a Wendy's restaurant in Brampton, Ontario, on April 21, 2026. Mike Campbell | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buy Wendy's, according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer. The Wall Street Journal first reported Peltz's proposal.Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines. Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain."In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.Trian previously explored a takeover of Wendy's in 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

schema.headline: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain

title: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
description: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC,
body: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.Here are five key takeaways:No surprises: Markets had been widely expecting the Fed to hold, and it did just that. In explaining its decision, the Federal Open Market Committee emphasized a patient approach, saying, "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."Well, one surprise: If there was one eyebrow-raising moment from the afternoon, it was Warsh's disclosure of changes in how the FOMC will meet. In 2027, the committee will still meet eight times, but one of the meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates, or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the next year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — outside of emergency meetings.OK, two surprises: The FOMC vote to hold policy where it stands was widely expected. Dissent from multiple members also came as no shock. But one of the "no" votes coming from Governor Lisa Cook was a stunner. Governors rarely dissent from rate votes, and Cook hasn't done so at all since taking her seat in 2022. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also opposed the decision. Both likely will provide statements explaining their votes before the end of the week.The AI impact: Warsh took the opportunity to talk about the impact artificial intelligence is having on economic growth, essentially saying that it was just one of several factors driving an expansion that he said was running strong.More musical chairs: The September meeting featured a shortened post-meeting news conference — cut from the usual 45 minutes or so down to half an hour, about the time of Wednesday's event. Moreover, reporters have been limited to a single question, a switch from prior practices when media members would take a two-for-one approach. Finally, Warsh has changed the seating in the room, going from a largely arbitrary approach — with representatives of larger outfits up front — to alphabetical order last month. This month featured reverse alphabetical order, keeping the bearers of the microphone on their toes.What they're saying:"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management."The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management."We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies.

schema.headline: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference

title: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment
description: A FedEx delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, July 25, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earning
body: A FedEx delivery truck is seen in Chicago, Illinois, July 25, 2026.Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earnings that beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines and raised its full-year outlook for its newly realigned fiscal year. Shares of the company fell slightly in extended trading.Here's how the company performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.74 adjusted vs. $3.36 expectedRevenue: $22.86 billion vs. $22.42 billion expectedThe company reported net income for the quarter of $290 million, or $1.21 per share, compared with $650 million, or $2.73 per share, during the comparable period a year prior. Adjusting for one-time items — including losses related to short-term investments, gains on the extinguishment of debt and certain restructuring costs — FedEx reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.74. It marks the first report of FedEx's realigned fiscal year, moving the end of its calendar from May 31 to Dec. 31. The report also comes after the company successfully spun out FedEx Freight into a separate publicly traded company. FedEx said its express U.S. segment operating income increased in the quarter, primarily driven by higher package yields and volume. "As our strong operating results and adjusted free cash flow demonstrate, FedEx is winning across high-value market segments while we optimize our network, driving an increase to our full-year outlook," CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a statement.For the full year, the company is now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $18 and $18.60, compared with a prior range of $16.90 to $18.10. FedEx also said it's revising its 2026 revenue growth expectation to a roughly 12% year-over-year increase, up from previous guidance of an 11% increase.Earlier this week, FedEx named former AutoZone executive Jamere Jackson as the company's new chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He replaces Claude Russ, who served as the interim CFO since June 1. John Dietrich was announced as stepping down from that role in April.

schema.headline: FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment

title: Chipotle shares rise 7% after CEO says same-store sales growth will continue
description: Chipotle Mexican Grill sign outside the chain's restaurant in the Mission Rock development, San Francisco, California, October 15, 2026. (Smith Collec
body: Chipotle Mexican Grill sign outside the chain's restaurant in the Mission Rock development, San Francisco, California, October 15, 2026. (Smith Collection/gado | Archive Photos | Getty ImagesChipotle Mexican Grill on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results and said its restaurant-level operating margin shrank.But the burrito chain saw traffic and same-store sales grow during the quarter as low-income consumers spent more, bucking industry trends, and CEO Scott Boatwright projected a strong finish to the year. Shares of the company rose 7% in extended trading."Broader consumer and industry headwinds may continue, but initiatives across our recipe for growth strategy are building and giving us more tools to win in any environment," Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call. "We are still in the early stages of this work, and it's gaining traction."Like the broader restaurant industry, Chipotle saw trends soften in early October, although executives said its traffic has returned to growth since then. Boatwright said the company has "high confidence" in its performance for the rest of the fourth quarter."We feel very confident that November and December set up very well for us," Boatwright said. Chief Financial Officer Adam Rymer said the company expects fourth-quarter same-store sales growth of about 2%.Here's what the company reported for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: 27 cents adjusted vs. 29 cents expectedRevenue: $3.29 billion vs. $3.29 billion expectedChipotle reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $339.9 million, or 27 cents per share, down from $382.1 million, or 29 cents per share, a year earlier. The company's restaurant-level operating margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%.Excluding restaurant asset impairment charges and stock-based compensation, the company earned 27 cents per share.Net sales rose 9.6% to $3.29 billion, fueled by the chain's new restaurants. During the quarter, Chipotle opened 84 company-owned restaurants and five international locations run by licensees. In the second half of July, Chipotle said it started to see sales pull back as diners grew concerned about consuming raw lettuce due to cyclospora, although its own supply was never tied to an outbreak. Then in August, the chain disclosed that it had temporarily pulled jalapenos from Minnesota restaurants after learning its supply was potentially linked to a salmonella outbreak. Still, the chain was able to report same-store sales growth for its third straight quarter, shaking off last year's traffic woes. Sales at stores open at least 13 months increased 2.1%, lifted by a 1.3% bump in average check. For the first time this year, low-income consumers during the quarter outperformed the high-income cohort at its restaurants, Boatwright said. And discounts aren't the reason — low-income consumers spent the most in September, when promotions were at their low point during the quarter, he told analysts.For the full year, Chipotle reiterated its previous forecast that its same-store sales will increase by a low-single-digit percentage. Looking ahead to 2027, the company is projecting that it will open between 340 and 360 new company-owned locations in the U.S. and Canada and around 15 to 25 international restaurants.

schema.headline: Chipotle shares rise 7% after CEO says same-store sales growth will continue

title: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket
description: Villa Vie Residences' Odyssey cruise ship passengers sit on an EV vehicle at a hotel in Sihanoukville, Preah Sihanouk province, on October 28, 2026. A
body: Villa Vie Residences' Odyssey cruise ship passengers sit on an EV vehicle at a hotel in Sihanoukville, Preah Sihanouk province, on October 28, 2026. Around 200 passengers who paid to live on a cruise ship while travelling the world were abruptly left in a Cambodian port after the company ran out of money, an official said on October 28. (Photo by TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images)Tang Chhin Sothy | Afp | Getty ImagesA luxury cruise around the world has abruptly stopped, stranding passengers in Cambodia, as its operator blamed skyrocketing fuel costs.The Villa Vie Odyssey, a luxury vessel with rooms costing up to $11,000 a month, will disembark passengers and crew and find temporary accommodation, per a Tuesday online release.The vessel can carry up to 650 passengers, according to its U.S.-based operator Villa Vie Residences, and has been on a continuous voyage around the world for two years since it departed Belfast, Northern Ireland.Its amenities include a fitness center and spa, a business center, three restaurants, five bars and lounges and complimentary alcoholic beverages.The cruise drew international attention as it was marketed as a residential cruise offering a permanent home at sea while visiting hundreds of destinations.An aerial view shows the Villa Vie Residences' cruise ship Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville port in Preah Sihanouk province on October 28, 2026. Around 200 passengers who paid to live on a cruise ship while travelling the world were abruptly left in a Cambodian port after the company ran out of money, an official said on October 28. (Photo by Suy Se / AFP via Getty Images)Suy Se | Afp | Getty ImagesThe ship was due to arrive at Phu Quoc, a Vietnamese island, later this week, and from there travel to destinations including India, South Africa, Brazil and Australia, before docking in Gibraltar in August 2030."Extraordinary increases" in fuel costs meant the company would need to restructure and recapitalize its business over the next 60 days, Villa Vie Residences said in an online statement. "No outcome is assured," it added.The company said monthly fuel costs per cabin had risen from $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia, which represents a 344% rise, according to CNBC's calculations."The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," the statement said.It added that, since the Iran war began on Feb. 28, "we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port.""Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs," the company added.- CNBC's Celia Fernandez contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket

title: Hands-on with Apple's first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional
description: watch nowApple announced its first touchscreen laptop models on Wednesday at an event in Los Angeles.These new MacBooks, called MacBook Pro with ProLE
body: watch nowApple announced its first touchscreen laptop models on Wednesday at an event in Los Angeles.These new MacBooks, called MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display, are still Apple MacBooks. They run MacOS, not iPadOS or iOS, the iPhone's operating system. Here's the good news for anyone who is worried about the new user interface: You don't have to use it. Touch is entirely optional. CNBC briefly tested both the 14-inch and 16-inch touchscreen MacBooks at the event. Users can still primarily or entirely use the device's trackpad and keyboard, and there are few visual updates. MacOS still looks largely the same as it used to.Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.Andrew Evers | CNBCThere have been a few user interface updates. For example, the red button on the top left of a window expands when you touch it to make it easier to click. Apple says that third-party developers like Microsoft and Adobe can and will update their apps to expand buttons and other touch targets to be larger. I think that touch will be particularly useful to scroll through websites or documents while lying down. But even software that hasn't been explicitly updated for the new computer will support touch. Apple says that behind the scenes, its software converts every touch tap into a traditional click. So any button that can be clicked can also be touched. Using the laptop with your finger feels good, but it won't change the way most people use their laptops. It could be useful for iPhone app developers, who can now test the way their apps work on their Mac. An accessibility feature allows users to pinch to zoom on any part of the user interface.Apple said on Wednesday that it had used an oleophobic coating on its screens to resist fingerprints. It appears to work. I didn't notice marks on the screen when I used the touch features.Apple is also, in addition to the touch feature, marketing these laptops as having a superior display, thanks to its new tandem OLED technology that offers deeper blacks and higher contrast. While photos and other art looked great on the screen, it's not a night-and-day difference from past Apple laptops. A lot of the improvements are aimed at creators who need accurate colors for photo and video editing. Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display and 12MP Center Stage camera.Andrew Evers | CNBCInstead of the notch at the top of previous MacBooks, where Apple hides its cameras, the new MacBooks have a hole-punch cutout in the display, like recent iPhones. Apple's Dynamic Island feature — new to the MacBook — expands to show live activities and Siri. Apple made a big deal about the laptop's new hinge, which is meant to keep the screen from shaking when you touch it. For example, if you tap the screen on a video call, your camera won't shake as much. But the hinge feels largely the same as Apple's previous MacBook Pros. There is one new feature that is immediately noticeable and tells people you bought the latest, greatest, and most expensive Apple laptop. (The smaller 14-inch model starts at $2,899 and the bigger one costs at least $3,399.) The Apple logo on the lid now lights up when the computer is on. It's the first Apple laptop that supports it since the 2017 MacBook Air.Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro.Andrew Evers | CNBCThe light-up logo drew a cheer from analysts and influencers in attendance when it was announced on Wednesday.

schema.headline: Hands-on with Apple's first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional

title: Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit
description: U.S. President Donald Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 22, 2026 in Washington,
body: U.S. President Donald Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. Alex Wong | Getty ImagesThree media outlets that President Donald Trump banned from the White House in September, only to have a federal judge's order restore much of their access, amended their lawsuit Wednesday, seeking to regain full access to serve in a press pool for other reporters in the Oval Office and Air Force One.The amended civil complaint against Trump says that since the judge ordered the White House to allow MS NOW, CNN and Politico journalists into the White House, the White House has blocked those outlets from performing pool functions they long have conducted.The press pool routinely serves as a key source of information for the public about what a president does or says. In pool assignments, journalists agree to share with other media outlets information and images they obtain while acting as a pooler.The amended complaint sets the stage for a court fight over whether a president, because of how he or she feels about how a media outlet covers them, can block access to individual media outlets or reporters from areas of the White House that other journalists have access to.Ted Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, in a statement Wednesday said, "Despite two court orders restraining it from implementing the President's unconstitutional ban on CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, the White House has continued to violate the First Amendment and due process by excluding those news organizations from areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One — the very locations that the President most frequently engages with the press.""These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn't like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people," Boutrous said. The amended complaint in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. says that Trump's original ban and "the White House's continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain [areas] are unlawful retaliation for protected First Amendment activity."Those actions "brazenly" discriminate against the outlets "based on their perceived editorial viewpoint; the White House is expressly excluding CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO because the President dislikes the content of their coverage," the suit says.Judge Tim Kelly's prior orders restoring access for the outlets did not require the White House to restore those outlets' access to the Oval Office or Air Force One.The amended complaint notes that since his second term began in January 2025, Trump has held 121 press events aboard Air Force One or on the tarmac outside the presidential plane, and 138 events in the Oval Office, "during which he fielded no fewer than 4,700 questions from reporters.""To be clear, Plaintiffs do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One," the new complaint says. "But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude Plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage."Members of the media report from Pebble Beach, the stand-up area for members of the media on the North Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSince Trump announced the ban on Sept. 18, "the White House has repeatedly barred CNN from fulfilling its duties as designated television network pooler aboard Air Force One — a role CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades," the amended suit says.MS NOW has not participated in the secondary TV pool since that date, and the White House has barred Politico "from two scheduled out-of-town print pool assignments aboard Air Force One," the suit says."Defendants have offered no official explanation for any of these exclusions," the amended complaint says."On information and belief, these exclusions reflect an unstated policy to carry out the President's directive to take his viewpoint-discriminatory and retaliatory ban 'as far as you can,'" the complaint says."Indeed, the President has been explicit that he intends to limit access to the Oval Office to news organizations that cover him favorably, declaring hours after this action was filed that 'publications that only write negatively . . . shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," the suit said.The suit notes that after Kelly issued a preliminary injunction against Trump's ban  in mid-October, "the White House issued a statement declaring that what it deems the 'Fake News' has 'no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office.'"President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One en route to Alaska on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesThe amended complaint says the limited ban on pool access violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution."CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO, and their journalists have liberty and property interests in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford to the White House grounds to report on the President and his administration," the suit says. "That access has long extended to the Oval Office, Air Force One, and other fora that the White House has opened to the press for pool coverage.""The ban, and Defendants' continued exclusion of Plaintiffs from certain White House press areas, deprives Plaintiffs of those interests without meeting the bare minimum requirements of due process: advance notice based on clear standards and an opportunity to be heard," the suit says.The suit also said the White House is interfering with CNN's ability to perform its duties as one of five television networks that "staff, equip, and bear the costs associated with the primary television network pool upon which the American public (and the White House itself) relies for real-time television coverage of the President in the Oval Office, aboard Air Force One, and at the many other presidential events that due to size and other constraints simply cannot accommodate all members of the press corps."Trump, when he announced the ban, said he was "sick" of what he called fiction and lies written about him, his administration, and the United States.On Sept. 19, a day after he announced the ban, journalists from the three media outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their passes taken away when they showed up.Two days later, the outlets first sued Trump, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Chief of Staff Susan Wiles, and Secret Service Director Sean Curran, seeking to regain access.District Court Judge Tim Kelly on Sept. 23 issued a temporary restraining order mandating that the White House restore access to the outlets for at least 14 days. Kelly, whom Trump appointed to the federal bench in 2017, said in his order that the ban appeared to flatly violate two federal appeals court rulings that require advance notice and an opportunity to be heard to journalists whose White House press passes are targeted for revocation.The White House allowed journalists from the banned outlets in the next day.On Oct. 13, Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, which indefinitely bars the White House from reinstituting the ban while the outlets' lawsuit continues in his court.In issuing that injunction, Kelly again cited the appeals court decisions, but also said the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which alleged retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

schema.headline: Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit

title: Nvidia's $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal draws DOJ scrutiny
description: Jensen Huang, co-founder, president and CEO of Nvidia, gestures during a press briefing in Paris on Oct. 13, 2026.Joel Saget | AFP | Getty ImagesNvidi
body: Jensen Huang, co-founder, president and CEO of Nvidia, gestures during a press briefing in Paris on Oct. 13, 2026.Joel Saget | AFP | Getty ImagesNvidia is facing questions from the U.S. Department of Justice concerning its acquisition of Hugging Face, an open-source platform for hosting and testing AI models, and how that deal may impact competitors in the field.CNBC has confirmed the probe with a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Reuters first reported the DOJ's inquiry on Wednesday. Nvidia announced its nearly $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face in September, and at the time, CEO Jensen Huang wrote that the deal would help "expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide."Hugging Face already had massive adoption. At the time of the deal, Nvidia said in a press statement that more than 18 million people and more than 200,000 companies reportedly used Hugging Face to share at least 3 million models and 500,000 datasets.Hugging Face also sells infrastructure and collaboration tools to organizations working with closed, proprietary AI including chip companies. The Hugging Face acquisition marked Nvidia's second-biggest purchase, after it paid $20 billion for Groq assets at the end of last year, a deal that has also attracted DOJ scrutiny. The closest comparable to Hugging Face's business was GitHub, a software repository that was acquired by Microsoft in 2018 for $7.5 billion. Hugging Face gained renewed recognition after reports that OpenAI agents attacked the platform during testing.The company and that incident are part of a new, Netflix "insta-documentary" called "AI Gone Rogue."Nvidia declined to comment.

schema.headline: Nvidia's $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal draws DOJ scrutiny

title: 10-year Treasury yield creeps higher even as Fed keeps rates the same
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., August 4, 2026. Jeenah Moon | ReutersBond yields moved higher
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., August 4, 2026. Jeenah Moon | ReutersBond yields moved higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points higher at 5.026%.The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, slipped more than 3 basis points to 4.704%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 4 basis points to 5.354%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the bank remained focused on "price stability" despite the pause and that the employment picture has been "quite positive."Despite the hold for October, expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 85.7%, according to CME's FedWatch tool.More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.That data will be critical to determining where the Fed may go from here, according to TruStage chief economist Steve Rick. "Holding rates steady doesn't necessarily mean the Fed is finished raising them, especially if inflation doesn't start to cool," he said. "Policymakers will want to see whether these price pressures are temporary or becoming more widespread throughout the economy."— CNBC's Alex Harring contributed reporting.

schema.headline: 10-year Treasury yield creeps higher even as Fed keeps rates the same

title: Fed leaves rates unchanged: What it means for credit cards, mortgages, auto loans and savings accounts
description: watch nowThe Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, even as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated and
body: watch nowThe Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, even as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated and further strain already-tight household budgets.Higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war may prove stickier than expected, but the central bank's decision to hold rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess the economic fallout. The dynamic could also lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee to consider raising rates at their December meeting in order to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target.For now, however, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs are compounding affordability challenges for many households, economists say.Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said in a post on Oct. 12 that the war has cost the average American household about $2,000 so far, mostly due to higher energy costs, in addition to heightened interest rate costs."High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto," Zandi told CNBC. "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders."How the Fed impacts your moneyThe Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline, means consumers are unlikely to see much relief from high borrowing costs anytime soon.The Fed influences the federal funds rate, an interest rate benchmark that sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending. That rate ripples throughout the economy, influencing both consumer borrowing costs and returns on savings.Short-term consumer lending rates, such as credit cards, closely track the prime rate, which typically moves in tandem with the Fed's benchmark and is generally about 3 percentage points higher. Longer-term rates, like those on 30-year mortgages, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and the economic outlook.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Credit cards provide one of the clearest examples of the Fed's influence. Because most cards have variable rates, borrowers typically see changes in the federal funds rate passed on within one to two billing cycles.But even as the Fed's benchmark rate has largely held steady — except for September's 25-basis-point increase — the average credit card interest rate has been trending higher amid concerns of rising delinquencies in the face of stubborn inflation, according to LendingTree."Credit card rates have risen for three straight months and are now at their highest levels since December 2025," said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief consumer finance analyst. "Rates are highly likely to rise in the next few months, too, as card issuers implement the Fed's September hike," he added.A sign is posted in front of a home for sale in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 3, 2026.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesUnlike credit cards and other variable-rate loans, 15- and 30-year fixed mortgage rates don't move in lockstep with the Fed's benchmark rate. Instead, they generally track long-term Treasury yields, which have recently climbed amid concerns that ongoing U.S.-Iran tensions and higher energy costs could keep inflation elevated. As a result, 30-year fixed mortgage rates have remained above 7% for more than a month, according to Mortgage News Daily. "There is no single switch that will bring mortgage rates meaningfully lower," said Jeff DerGurahian, LoanDepot's chief investment officer and head economist. "We likely need several factors to fall into place, including cooler oil prices, softer consumer spending and a steady run of inflation reports showing progress toward the Fed's 2% target."Meanwhile, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that aims to reduce some mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable.A Cadillac dealership in Colma, California, Jan. 23, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAuto loan rates are fixed for the life of the loan, and market rates are tied to several factors, including the Fed's benchmark. "The headline new-car APR has essentially flatlined at the 7% threshold all year," according to Joseph Yoon, senior analyst at Edmunds. Without a rate hike, car buyers may be offered lower rates on auto loans in the weeks ahead, but only temporarily as dealers roll out special year-end financing offers, he said. "If that number ticks down over the next two months, it won't be because the broader lending environment suddenly turned loose," he said. "Historically, the fourth quarter creates an artificial sense of rate relief because automakers and their captive finance branches start lowering interest rates to move outgoing cars before December 31."And yet, the "big catch," Yoon added, is that subsidized holiday rates are largely reserved for new car shoppers with top-tier credit. "For everyone else — particularly shoppers browsing the used-car lots where interest rates continue to hold above 10% — the high cost of borrowing isn't budging anytime soon," he said. Federal student loan rates are also fixed for the life of the loan, so most borrowers are somewhat shielded from Fed moves. However, rates for new borrowers are already higher based on the results of the 10-year Treasury note auction held in May. Currently, interest rates for new federal student loans range from 6.52% to 9.07%, depending on the loan type.On Saturday, Trump said he "might" support legislation capping federal student loan interest rates in the future. The bill, introduced by Reps. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., and Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., is still in committee. Savings rates tend to be correlated with changes in the target federal funds rate. Although holding the Fed's rate unchanged has kept savings yields largely steady, some top-yielding online savings accounts can offer above-average returns and currently pay more than 4%, according to Bankrate."Now is a great time to shop around for a high-yield savings account to take advantage of today's high rates," Schulz said. "The returns are below the record highs of a few years ago, but they're still far greater than what you can get from a traditional savings account with a giant megabank."The bottom lineFor many households, the Fed's most significant impact comes through its efforts to keep inflation in check, economists say.When higher interest rates help slow price growth, consumers may find it easier to afford everyday necessities such as groceries and gas."The Fed cannot drill for oil, but it can make borrowing more expensive. Higher rates can restrain demand and limit businesses' ability to pass along costs," said Sung Won Sohn, professor of finance and economics at Loyola Marymount University and chief economist at SS Economics.However, elevated borrowing costs can intensify affordability challenges for consumers. Some experts suggest consumers can help offset some of that strain by paying down high-interest debt, negotiating better loan terms and taking advantage of higher yields on savings."These steps can also improve access to more favorable financing options should interest rates moderate in the future," said Charlie Wise, head of global research and consulting at TransUnion.Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: Fed leaves rates unchanged: What it means for credit cards, mortgages, auto loans and savings accounts

title: The 'Magnificent Seven' is no more. Time to pick winners and losers as group's correlation breaks down
description: Jakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesThe "Magnificent Seven" doesn't trade as a monolith anymore, challenging investors to be more discerning when
body: Jakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesThe "Magnificent Seven" doesn't trade as a monolith anymore, challenging investors to be more discerning when picking through the market's biggest stocks rather than viewing them as a single trade. CNBC calculated the rolling 60-day correlation of daily returns for each of the 21 unique pairs among the Magnificent Seven — which comprises Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla.The average of those correlations recently fell to its lowest level in more than a decade, suggesting the group is trading less like a cohesive block than it has historically. This marks a departure for a group that's often discussed together because of its size and influence over the broader market.The companies "all have different exposures to AI," said Gil Luria, analyst at D.A. Davidson. "This requires a much more granular approach to which of the largest mega-caps an investor wants to own as opposed to just owning them wholesale," he added.The dislocation has led the group as a whole to lag the broader market. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS) is up 7% year to date, while the S&P 500 has gained 12%. Tesla and Meta are the two names in the cohort down in 2026, while Nvidia and Apple are the only ones outperforming the S&P 500.Microsoft and Alphabet report results after the bell Wednesday. Amazon will post earnings after the close on Thursday.The growing divergence among the Magnificent Seven reflects investors' deeper focus on companies' "independent fundamental growth drivers," said Thomas DiFazio, ETF strategist at Roundhill Investments. "They have varying levels of success, when you put them in the totem pole of AI winners and losers."He added that "investors are focusing on the micro factors," such as company-specific news that can signal whether the business can flourish in the AI world. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconMAGS ETF vs S&P 500 YTDFor Microsoft, the market is watching Azure's cloud growth. For Meta, it's assessing the potential of its consumer AI applications. Apple's appeal is with its devices and services. Meanwhile, Alphabet's success is tied to its Google Cloud business, its AI model Gemini and its leadership in Search. Close eyes are also on Amazon's cloud business growth, while the market is centered on evaluating the durability of demand for Nvidia's chips. For Tesla, it's less about electric vehicles and more about its pivot to AI, robotics and robotaxis —potentially in a merger with SpaceX. "These are the best stocks to still be in, but they're starting to kind of separate and go in their own direction," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets.The dispersion within the Magnificent Seven doesn't point to deteriorating fundamentals. Overall, Wall Street remains largely bullish on each individual stock. For Apple, 58% of analysts have a buy or strong buy rating on the stock, according to LSEG. That number is a whopping 97% for Amazon; 92% for Alphabet; 97% on Microsoft; 89% on Meta; 97% on Nvidia; and 50% on Tesla. AppleApple illustrates how investors' assessment of AI exposure has shifted.The iPhone maker, which had been punished for not spending high levels of capital expenditures in the AI arms race, is now being rewarded for it. In 2025, Apple was the second worst-performing Magnificent Seven name, returning 8.9%. Amazon was in last place, gaining 5.2% in 2025. Alphabet was the best performer, delivering 65.8%. In 2026, however, Apple's 28% gain leads the Mag-7 pack.Performance of each Magnificent Seven stockTicker Company Year-to-date performance (%) GOOGLAlphabet2.2AMZNAmazon8.8AAPLApple26.8METAMeta Platforms-5.2MSFTMicrosoft10.7NVDANvidia17.3TSLATesla-10.8Source: FactSet"The one stock that got criticized the most over the last two years about not having an AI strategy is now the leader of this cohort, and that is Apple," Woods said."They're continuing to hit on what they do best, which is the products and the App Store," Woods explained. To him, Apple is the "consistent tortoise of this race."D.A. Davidson's Luria described Apple as "the place to hide from the AI trade," while Woods referred to the company as a "technology utility" and a "consumer staple" since its devices and services are embedded into everyday life.NvidiaNvidia has been volatile lately amid concerns about the durability of chip demand and investor anxiety over a pullback in capex spending.As the biggest stock in the semiconductor sector – and the world – the stock is bound to be subject to massive price swings. The stock peaked on Oct. 6 but since then, shares have fallen by over 13%. Still, Woods said its valuation is "relatively [and] historically cheap." Right now, the stock is in a "digestion phase." He favors Nvidia's setup, pointing to continued demand for chips. AlphabetAlphabet's chart has weakened following its run from March to May, according to Woods, putting greater emphasis on earnings and guidance come Wednesday evening when the company reports its third quarter earnings.While its search business remains a strength, Woods is watching competition from other AI platforms and whether the stock can gain upward momentum.AmazonAmazon has been "slow and steady," but the stock's trend hasn't been consistent, said Woods. "It's not doing poorly; it's not doing great. It's just there."The key for the company is its cloud computing business, Amazon Web Services, which deliver a majority of its profits. Revenue from Amazon's cloud segment grew 37% year over year in the second quarter. While growth is solid, it lagged Azure's 43% year over year growth last quarter and Google Cloud, which jumped 82% year over year last quarter. To be fair, AWS is much bigger than the other cloud-computing competitors and that growth rate was the largest for the segment in 18 quarters.Meta PlatformsMeta stock surged in September on excitement over its new personal AI assistant Muse after App Store downloads were off the charts. Roundhill's DiFazio noted how investors are keen on how Muse adoption could translate into revenue and profits and credited the new consumer application with potentially helping the stock's trajectory.But after the Facebook and Instagram parent reported negative free cash flow while raising the floor of its full-year capital expenditures in its third quarter earnings last week, the stock turned negative over concerns that attracrtive returns on all its capex could be further away. MicrosoftMicrosoft has recovered from earlier concerns about AI disrupting its software business, but now faces a technical test, according to Woods. "The fears that AI was going to disrupt this thought were definitely overblown," Woods said. He identified the $530-$550 range as resistance and said that selling pressure could potentially threaten further gains. DiFazio identified Azure as the growth driver investors are watching.Upcoming earnings and guidance, set to be delivered on Wednesday evening, can help determine whether the stock can break above that range.TeslaWhen discussing Magnificent Seven stocks, Tesla "has been left in the dust," Woods said. Tesla's investment case increasingly rests on opportunities beyond electric cars, including robotics, he said. D.A. Davidson's Luria is also skeptical of its inclusion in the Magnificent Seven, arguing its valuation carries an "Elon premium."— CNBC's Nick Wells contributed reporting.
